terms.grammar: phrase: ignōrō, ignōrāre, ignōrāvī, ignōrātum with nōn, and an object, an accusative and infinitive or an indirect question
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.11.1: nōn ignōrō quantum ex dēsīderiō labōrēs
terms.comment: Latin says “I am not unaware”: nōn ignōrō, and in the same way nōn sum nescius (Cic. Fam. 13.7.1). Plain sciō will often do (see know).

terms.grammar: verb, fourth conjugation, transitive: with an object or an accusative and infinitive
terms.comment: Awareness through the senses or the mind: to feel, to notice, to realise (see feel, notice). It also means to think, to hold an opinion (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: adjective: with the genitive, or an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Plaut. Rud. 1.3.28 (Lewis & Short): nec locī gnāra sum
terms.comment: Rare but classical (Lewis & Short), with the genitive of what one knows; its opposite ignārus, unaware, is common: ignārus sua sē tractāre perīcla (Ov. M. 8.195–200).

terms.grammar: phrase: the person in the accusative (certiōrem, certiōrēs), the matter with dē or an accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. Fam. 13.77.1: velim faciās eōs per litterās certiōrēs
terms.comment: “To make someone more certain”: Cicero’s and Caesar’s phrase for informing someone. Passive certior fīō, I learn, I am told.

phrases.latin: nōn ignōrō quantum ex dēsīderiō labōrēs; sed erunt omnia facilia sī valēbis.
phrases.english: I’m well aware how much you suffer from missing us; but everything will be easy if you get well.

phrases.latin: puer Īcarus ūnā stābat et, ignārus sua sē tractāre perīcla, ōre renīdentī modo, quās vaga mōverat aura, captābat plūmās
phrases.english: the boy Icarus stood beside him and, unaware that he was handling his own doom, with a beaming face snatched at the feathers the wandering breeze had stirred

sources: Lewis & Short: ignoro · Lewis & Short: sentio · Lewis & Short: gnarus · Lewis & Short: certus
